name: Gluteus maximus
etymology: From Greek gloutos ‘buttock’ + Latin maximus ‘largest’. So it means ‘the largest buttock muscle’ — the big superficial mass that shapes the buttock.
origin: Posterior ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, dorsal surface of sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, thoracolumbar fascia
insertion: Iliotibial tract (most fibres) and gluteal tuberosity of femur
actions: Stabilises the knee in extension via the IT tract
tip: Most active in powerful extension from flexion (stairs, squat lock-out, sprinting) rather than in level walking.

name: Gluteus medius
etymology: From Greek gloutos ‘buttock’ + Latin medius ‘middle’. So it means ‘the middle buttock muscle’ — middle in size and depth, between maximus and minimus.
origin: External surface of ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines
insertion: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter
actions: Stabilises the pelvis in single-leg stance
Hip internal rotation and flexion (anterior fibres)
Hip external rotation and extension (posterior fibres)
tip: Weakness gives a positive Trendelenburg sign — the pelvis drops on the opposite side when standing on the weak leg.

name: Gluteus minimus
etymology: From Greek gloutos ‘buttock’ + Latin minimus ‘smallest’. So it means ‘the smallest buttock muscle’ — the deepest of the three glutes.
origin: External surface of ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
insertion: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter
actions: Stabilises the pelvis in single-leg stance
tip: Works with glute med as a pelvic stabiliser; its tendon is a common site of lateral hip (greater trochanteric) pain.

name: Tensor fasciae latae
etymology: From Latin tensor ‘stretcher, tightener’ + fasciae ‘of the band’ + latae ‘broad’. So it means ‘tightener of the broad band’ — it tenses the fascia lata / IT band.
origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) and anterior part of the outer iliac crest
insertion: Iliotibial tract, which attaches to the lateral tibial condyle (Gerdy’s tubercle)
actions: Tenses the IT tract to stabilise the extended knee
tip: Often overactive when glute med is weak; tightness is linked to IT band syndrome on the lateral knee.

name: Piriformis
etymology: From Latin pirum ‘pear’ + forma ‘shape’. So it means ‘pear-shaped’ — a flat, tapering muscle passing out of the greater sciatic notch.
origin: Anterior surface of the sacrum (S2–S4 level) and margin of the greater sciatic notch
insertion: Superior border of the greater trochanter
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
tip: The sciatic nerve usually exits just below it (sometimes through it), so a tight piriformis can mimic sciatica — ‘piriformis syndrome’.

name: Superior gemellus
etymology: From Latin superior ‘upper’ + gemellus ‘little twin’ (diminutive of geminus ‘twin’). So it means ‘the upper little twin’ — paired with the inferior gemellus above and below the obturator internus tendon.
origin: Ischial spine (outer surface)
insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter, blending with the obturator internus tendon
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
tip: One of the ‘deep six’ hip external rotators: piriformis, gemellus superior, obturator internus, gemellus inferior, quadratus femoris, obturator externus.

name: Obturator internus
etymology: From Latin obturare ‘to stop up, block’ + internus ‘inner’. So it means ‘the inner muscle of the blocked opening’ — it arises from the inside of the obturator membrane that closes the obturator foramen.
origin: Inner (pelvic) surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone of the obturator foramen
insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter (after turning around the lesser sciatic notch)
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
tip: Its tendon makes a sharp turn through the lesser sciatic foramen, and its fascia also forms part of the pelvic side wall.

name: Inferior gemellus
etymology: From Latin inferior ‘lower’ + gemellus ‘little twin’. So it means ‘the lower little twin’ — the lower partner of the superior gemellus.
origin: Upper part of the ischial tuberosity
insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter, blending with the obturator internus tendon
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
tip: Note the nerve split: superior gemellus goes with obturator internus, inferior gemellus with quadratus femoris.

name: Quadratus femoris
etymology: From Latin quadratus ‘squared, four-sided’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’. So it means ‘the square muscle of the thigh’ — a flat rectangular block below the gemelli.
origin: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity
insertion: Quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
tip: The lowest of the deep rotators seen from behind; can be pinched between ischium and femur (ischiofemoral impingement).

name: Obturator externus
etymology: From Latin obturare ‘to stop up, block’ + externus ‘outer’. So it means ‘the outer muscle of the blocked opening’ — it covers the outside of the obturator membrane.
origin: External surface of the obturator membrane and surrounding bone of the obturator foramen
insertion: Trochanteric fossa of the femur
actions: Stabilises the femoral head in the acetabulum
tip: The only deep hip rotator supplied by the obturator nerve; it lies deep in the medial thigh, hidden by the adductors.

name: Iliacus
etymology: From Latin ilium / ilia ‘flank, groin’ (the hip bone’s wing) + -acus ‘belonging to’. So it means ‘the muscle of the ilium’ — it fills the iliac fossa.
origin: Iliac fossa, inner lip of the iliac crest and ala of the sacrum
insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (with the psoas major tendon)
tip: Joins psoas major to form the iliopsoas, the strongest hip flexor; tightness pulls the pelvis into anterior tilt.

name: Psoas major
etymology: From Greek psoa ‘loin muscles’ + Latin major ‘larger’. So it means ‘the larger loin muscle’ — the long muscle running from the lumbar spine down to the thigh.
origin: Sides of the T12–L5 vertebral bodies and intervening discs; transverse processes of L1–L5
insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur (with iliacus)
tip: With iliacus it forms the iliopsoas; a tight psoas increases lumbar lordosis — test with the Thomas test.

name: Sartorius
etymology: From Latin sartor ‘tailor’ (from sarcire ‘to patch, mend’). So it means ‘the tailor’s muscle’ — it produces the cross-legged position tailors sat in to sew.
origin: Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)
insertion: Superior medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
tip: Longest muscle in the body; pes anserinus order front-to-back is Sartorius, Gracilis, semiTendinosus — ‘Say Grace before Tea’.

name: Rectus femoris
etymology: From Latin rectus ‘straight’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’ (femur, thigh). So it means ‘the straight muscle of the thigh’ — its fibres run straight down the front of the thigh, unlike the oblique vasti.
origin: Anterior inferior iliac spine (straight head); superior acetabular rim (reflected head)
insertion: Base of patella via the quadriceps tendon, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
tip: The only quad that crosses the hip — stretch it with hip extension + knee flexion.

name: Vastus lateralis
etymology: From Latin vastus ‘vast, huge’ + lateralis ‘of the side’. So it means ‘the huge muscle on the outer side’ — the largest quadriceps head, on the lateral thigh.
origin: Greater trochanter, upper intertrochanteric line, gluteal tuberosity and lateral lip of the linea aspera
insertion: Lateral border of the patella and quadriceps tendon, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
tip: Largest quad head; a strong VL relative to VMO can pull the patella laterally.

name: Vastus medialis
etymology: From Latin vastus ‘vast, huge’ + medialis ‘of the middle (inner) side’. So it means ‘the huge muscle on the inner side’ — the teardrop-shaped quad above the medial knee.
origin: Lower intertrochanteric line, spiral line, medial lip of the linea aspera and medial supracondylar line
insertion: Medial border of the patella and quadriceps tendon, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
actions: Medial stabilisation of the patella (oblique fibres, VMO)
tip: Its lower oblique fibres (VMO) resist lateral patellar tracking — a classic focus in patellofemoral pain rehab.

name: Vastus intermedius
etymology: From Latin vastus ‘vast, huge’ + intermedius ‘lying between’. So it means ‘the huge muscle in between’ — it lies deep, between the other two vasti, under rectus femoris.
origin: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the femoral shaft (upper two-thirds)
insertion: Deep surface of the quadriceps tendon to the patella, then via the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity
tip: Hidden under rectus femoris; a small slip from it (articularis genus) lifts the knee joint capsule during extension.

name: Pectineus
etymology: From Latin pecten ‘comb’. So it means ‘the comb muscle’ — it arises from the pecten pubis, a comb-like ridge on the pubic bone.
origin: Pecten pubis (pectineal line of the superior pubic ramus)
insertion: Pectineal line of the femur, just below the lesser trochanter
innervation: Femoral nerve (L2–L3); sometimes a branch of the obturator nerve
tip: Forms part of the floor of the femoral triangle and is often strained along with adductor longus in groin injuries.

name: Adductor longus
etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ (ad ‘to’ + ducere ‘to lead’) + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long muscle that draws the leg in’ toward the midline.
origin: Body of the pubis, just below the pubic crest
insertion: Middle third of the linea aspera of the femur
tip: The most commonly strained adductor in ‘groin strains’; its tendon is the prominent cord you feel at the groin.

name: Adductor brevis
etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short muscle that draws the leg in’ — shorter than adductor longus, which lies in front of it.
origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
insertion: Pectineal line and upper part of the linea aspera of the femur
tip: Lies between the anterior and posterior divisions of the obturator nerve — a useful landmark.

name: Adductor magnus
etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ + magnus ‘great, large’. So it means ‘the great muscle that draws the leg in’ — the largest adductor, filling the back of the medial thigh.
origin: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus; hamstring part: ischial tuberosity
insertion: Adductor part: gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera and medial supracondylar line; hamstring part: adductor tubercle of the femur
innervation: Obturator nerve (adductor part, L2–L4); tibial division of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part, L4)
tip: Dual nerve supply because its hamstring part acts like a hamstring; the femoral vessels pass through its adductor hiatus.

name: Adductor minimus
etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ + minimus ‘smallest’. So it means ‘the smallest muscle that draws the leg in’ — a name for the uppermost slip of adductor magnus.
origin: Inferior pubic ramus (upper, most anterior fibres of adductor magnus)
insertion: Gluteal tuberosity and upper linea aspera of the femur
tip: Not a separate muscle in most texts — it is the upper, horizontal part of adductor magnus, often partly separated from it.

name: Gracilis
etymology: From Latin gracilis ‘slender, thin’. So it means ‘the slender muscle’ — a long, strap-like muscle down the inner thigh.
origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis
insertion: Superior medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
tip: The only adductor crossing the knee; middle tendon of the pes anserinus — ‘Say Grace before Tea’.

name: Biceps femoris
etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ (biceps ‘two-headed’) + femoris ‘of the thigh’. So it means ‘the two-headed muscle of the thigh’ — long and short heads join into one tendon.
origin: Long head: ischial tuberosity; short head: lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line
insertion: Head of the fibula
innervation: Sciatic nerve: tibial division (long head) and common fibular division (short head) (L5–S2)
tip: The lateral hamstring — its tendon is the cord on the outside back of the knee, and it’s a frequent site of sprinting strains.

name: Biceps femoris — long head
etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’; ‘long head’ is the longer of its two origins. So it is ‘the long head of the two-headed thigh muscle’, starting up at the sitting bone.
origin: Ischial tuberosity (common tendon with semitendinosus)
insertion: Head of the fibula (with the short head)
innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
tip: Crosses both hip and knee, so it is the most commonly strained hamstring in sprinting.

name: Biceps femoris — short head
etymology: From Latin bi- ‘two’ + caput ‘head’ + femoris ‘of the thigh’; ‘short head’ is the shorter origin. So it is ‘the short head of the two-headed thigh muscle’, starting on the femur shaft.
origin: Lateral lip of the linea aspera and lateral supracondylar line of the femur
insertion: Head of the fibula (with the long head)
innervation: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
tip: The only hamstring-group part that doesn’t cross the hip — and the only one supplied by the common fibular division.

name: Semitendinosus
etymology: From Latin semi ‘half’ + tendinosus ‘tendinous’. So it means ‘the half-tendon muscle’ — its lower half is a long, cord-like tendon.
origin: Ischial tuberosity (common tendon with the long head of biceps femoris)
insertion: Superior medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus)
innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
tip: Back tendon of the pes anserinus (‘Say Grace before Tea’) and a common ACL reconstruction graft.

name: Semimembranosus
etymology: From Latin semi ‘half’ + membranosus ‘membranous’. So it means ‘the half-membrane muscle’ — its upper part is a flat, sheet-like tendon.
origin: Ischial tuberosity (superolateral impression)
insertion: Posterior surface of the medial tibial condyle; expansions form the oblique popliteal ligament
innervation: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve (L5–S2)
tip: Lies deep to semitendinosus; its expansions also tension the posterior knee capsule and medial meniscus.

name: Tibialis anterior
etymology: From Latin tibia ‘shin bone’ (originally ‘flute’) + -alis ‘relating to’ + anterior ‘front’. So it means ‘the front shin-bone muscle’ — it lies along the front of the tibia.
origin: Lateral condyle and upper half to two-thirds of the lateral surface of the tibia; interosseous membrane
insertion: Medial and plantar surfaces of the medial cuneiform and base of the 1st metatarsal
tip: Overload causes anterior shin splints; weakness (e.g. deep fibular nerve palsy) gives foot drop. Anterior ankle order: ‘Tom Has A Very Nervous Eating Disorder’.

name: Extensor hallucis longus
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + hallucis ‘of the big toe’ (hallux) + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long extensor of the big toe’.
origin: Middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
insertion: Dorsal base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
tip: Testing big-toe extension strength is a quick screen of the L5 myotome. It is the ‘H’ in ‘Tom Has A Very Nervous Eating Disorder’.

name: Extensor digitorum longus
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + digitorum ‘of the digits’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long extensor of the toes’.
origin: Lateral condyle of the tibia, upper three-quarters of the anterior fibula and interosseous membrane
insertion: Middle and distal phalanges of toes 2–5 via the dorsal extensor expansions
tip: Its four tendons fan out across the dorsum of the foot; it is the ‘Eating Disorder’ (Extensor Digitorum) in ‘Tom Has A Very Nervous Eating Disorder’.

name: Fibularis tertius
etymology: From Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’ + -aris ‘relating to’ + tertius ‘third’. So it means ‘the third fibula muscle’ (peroneus is from Greek peronē ‘pin’, the same idea).
origin: Lower third of the anterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the 5th metatarsal
tip: Really a lower slip of extensor digitorum longus and absent in some people — unlike the other fibularis muscles it sits in the anterior compartment.

name: Fibularis longus
etymology: From Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’ + -aris ‘relating to’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long fibula muscle’ (peroneus from Greek peronē ‘pin’, the same bone).
origin: Head and upper two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
insertion: Plantar surfaces of the base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform (tendon crosses the sole in the cuboid groove)
actions: Supports the lateral longitudinal and transverse arches
tip: With tibialis anterior it forms a ‘stirrup’ under the foot; strengthen the fibularis muscles after lateral ankle sprains.

name: Fibularis brevis
etymology: From Latin fibula ‘clasp, brooch’ + -aris ‘relating to’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short fibula muscle’.
origin: Lower two-thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula
insertion: Tuberosity on the base of the 5th metatarsal
tip: A forceful inversion sprain can avulse its insertion — a 5th metatarsal base fracture.

name: Gastrocnemius
etymology: From Greek gastēr ‘belly’ + knēmē ‘leg, shin’. So it means ‘the belly of the leg’ — the bulging calf muscle.
origin: Medial head: posterior femur above the medial condyle; lateral head: lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle
insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
tip: Joins soleus to form the Achilles tendon (triceps surae); crosses the knee, so stretch it with the knee straight.

name: Gastrocnemius — medial head
etymology: From Greek gastēr ‘belly’ + knēmē ‘leg’, plus Latin medialis ‘of the inner side’. So it is ‘the inner head of the leg’s belly muscle’.
origin: Posterior surface of the femur just above the medial condyle
insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
tip: Larger and lower than the lateral head; ‘tennis leg’ is classically a tear of this head.

name: Gastrocnemius — lateral head
etymology: From Greek gastēr ‘belly’ + knēmē ‘leg’, plus Latin lateralis ‘of the side’. So it is ‘the outer head of the leg’s belly muscle’.
origin: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle
insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
tip: Often contains a small sesamoid bone (fabella) in its tendon behind the lateral knee.

name: Soleus
etymology: From Latin solea ‘sandal, sole’ (also the flatfish ‘sole’). So it means ‘the sole-shaped muscle’ — a broad, flat muscle under the gastrocnemius, probably named for its flatfish shape.
origin: Posterior head and upper shaft of the fibula, soleal line and medial border of the tibia, tendinous arch between them
insertion: Posterior calcaneus via the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
actions: Ankle plantarflexion (dominant when the knee is flexed)
Postural control of standing (prevents forward sway)
tip: Doesn’t cross the knee — target it with bent-knee calf raises and stretches; with gastrocnemius it forms the Achilles tendon.

name: Plantaris
etymology: From Latin planta ‘sole of the foot’ + -aris ‘relating to’. So it means ‘the muscle of the sole’ — in other animals it continues into the plantar fascia.
origin: Lateral supracondylar line of the femur and oblique popliteal ligament
insertion: Posterior calcaneus, medial to the calcaneal (Achilles) tendon
tip: Tiny belly with a very long thin tendon; absent in some people and harvested as a tendon graft.

name: Popliteus
etymology: From Latin poples ‘ham, back of the knee’. So it means ‘the muscle of the back of the knee’ — it lies in the floor of the popliteal fossa.
origin: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and lateral meniscus
insertion: Posterior surface of the tibia above the soleal line
actions: Unlocks the extended knee (femoral external rotation on fixed tibia / tibial internal rotation)
tip: The ‘key that unlocks the knee’ — it reverses the screw-home mechanism at the start of knee flexion.

name: Tibialis posterior
etymology: From Latin tibia ‘shin bone’ + -alis ‘relating to’ + posterior ‘back’. So it means ‘the back shin-bone muscle’ — the deepest muscle at the back of the leg.
origin: Interosseous membrane and adjacent posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula
insertion: Navicular tuberosity, plus cuneiforms, cuboid, sustentaculum tali and bases of metatarsals 2–4
tip: Dysfunction causes adult flatfoot; first structure behind the medial malleolus — ‘Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry’.

name: Flexor digitorum longus
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + digitorum ‘of the digits’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long flexor of the toes’.
origin: Medial part of the posterior surface of the tibia below the soleal line
insertion: Plantar bases of the distal phalanges of toes 2–5
tip: The ‘Dick’ in ‘Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry’ behind the medial malleolus; quadratus plantae and the lumbricals attach to its tendons.

name: Flexor hallucis longus
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + hallucis ‘of the big toe’ + longus ‘long’. So it means ‘the long flexor of the big toe’.
origin: Lower two-thirds of the posterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane
insertion: Plantar base of the distal phalanx of the great toe
tip: Key for push-off in walking and running (and dancers’ en pointe); the ‘Harry’ in ‘Tom, Dick And Very Nervous Harry’.

name: Extensor digitorum brevis
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + digitorum ‘of the digits’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short extensor of the toes’ — a small muscle on top of the foot.
origin: Superolateral surface of the calcaneus and inferior extensor retinaculum
insertion: Lateral sides of the long extensor tendons of toes 2–4
tip: The only muscle on the dorsum of the foot (with EHB) — the soft bulge in front of the lateral malleolus.

name: Extensor hallucis brevis
etymology: From Latin extensor ‘straightener’ + hallucis ‘of the big toe’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short extensor of the big toe’.
origin: Superolateral surface of the calcaneus (with extensor digitorum brevis)
insertion: Dorsal base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe
actions: Great toe extension at the MTP joint
tip: Essentially the medial slip of extensor digitorum brevis.

name: Abductor hallucis
etymology: From Latin abducere ‘to lead away’ (ab ‘away’ + ducere ‘to lead’) + hallucis ‘of the big toe’. So it means ‘the muscle that draws the big toe away’ from the second toe.
origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, flexor retinaculum and plantar aponeurosis
insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe
actions: Great toe flexion at the MTP joint
tip: Forms the medial border of the sole; a key ‘short foot’ exercise target for arch control and bunion management.

name: Flexor digitorum brevis
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + digitorum ‘of the digits’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short flexor of the toes’.
origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis
insertion: Both sides of the middle phalanges of toes 2–5
actions: Flexion of toes 2–5 at the PIP joints
tip: Its split tendons let the FDL tendons pass through to the distal phalanges — like FDS in the hand.

name: Abductor digiti minimi (foot)
etymology: From Latin abducere ‘to lead away’ + digiti ‘of the digit’ + minimi ‘smallest’. So it means ‘the muscle that draws the little toe away’ from the others.
origin: Medial and lateral processes of the calcaneal tuberosity and plantar aponeurosis
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th toe
actions: 5th toe flexion at the MTP joint
tip: Forms the lateral border of the sole.

name: Quadratus plantae
etymology: From Latin quadratus ‘squared, four-sided’ + plantae ‘of the sole’. So it means ‘the square muscle of the sole’.
origin: Medial and lateral surfaces of the plantar calcaneus (two heads)
insertion: Lateral margin of the flexor digitorum longus tendon
actions: Straightens the oblique pull of FDL
tip: Its alternative name ‘flexor accessorius’ says it all — a helper that redirects FDL’s pull in line with the toes.

name: Lumbricals (foot)
etymology: From Latin lumbricus ‘earthworm’. So it means ‘the worm-like muscles’ — four small slender muscles between the flexor tendons.
origin: Tendons of flexor digitorum longus
insertion: Medial sides of the dorsal extensor expansions of toes 2–5
actions: Flexion of toes 2–5 at the MTP joints
Extension of toes 2–5 at the IP joints
innervation: 1st: medial plantar nerve; 2nd–4th: lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
tip: Help keep the toes flat on the ground during push-off; weakness contributes to claw/hammer toes.

name: Flexor hallucis brevis
parts: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + hallucis ‘of the big toe’ + brevis ‘short’. So it means ‘the short flexor of the big toe’ — it has medial and lateral heads.
origin: Plantar surfaces of the cuboid and lateral cuneiform
insertion: Both sides of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe (each head via a sesamoid bone)
actions: Great toe flexion at the MTP joint
tip: Each head’s tendon contains a sesamoid under the 1st metatarsal head — irritation there is ‘sesamoiditis’.

name: Adductor hallucis
etymology: From Latin adducere ‘to lead towards’ + hallucis ‘of the big toe’. So it means ‘the muscle that draws the big toe in’ toward the second toe — it has oblique and transverse heads.
origin: Oblique head: bases of metatarsals 2–4; transverse head: plantar ligaments of MTP joints 3–5
insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe (via the lateral sesamoid)
actions: Great toe flexion at the MTP joint
innervation: Deep branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
tip: Its unopposed pull contributes to hallux valgus (bunion) deformity.

name: Flexor digiti minimi brevis (foot)
etymology: From Latin flexor ‘bender’ + digiti ‘of the digit’ + minimi ‘smallest’. So it means ‘the flexor of the little toe’.
origin: Base of the 5th metatarsal and sheath of the fibularis longus tendon
insertion: Lateral base of the proximal phalanx of the 5th toe
actions: 5th toe flexion at the MTP joint
innervation: Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve (S2–S3)
tip: Lies alongside abductor digiti minimi in the lateral compartment of the sole.

name: Opponens digiti minimi (foot)
aka: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of foot
parts: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of foot
etymology: From Latin opponens ‘placing against’ + digiti ‘of the digit’ + minimi ‘smallest’. So it means ‘the opposer of the little toe’ — named after its hand counterpart, though the toe can’t truly oppose.
origin: Long plantar ligament and sheath of the fibularis longus tendon
insertion: Lateral border of the 5th metatarsal
actions: Draws the 5th metatarsal medially and plantarward (deepens the lateral sole)
tip: Inconstant — many texts treat it as a deep slip of flexor digiti minimi brevis rather than a separate muscle.

name: Dorsal interossei (foot)
etymology: From Latin dorsalis ‘of the back’ + inter ‘between’ + ossa ‘bones’. So it means ‘the muscles between the bones, on the back (top) side’ — four bipennate muscles between the metatarsals.
origin: Adjacent sides of metatarsals 1–5 (two heads each)
insertion: Bases of the proximal phalanges and extensor expansions: 1st to medial side of 2nd toe, 2nd–4th to lateral sides of toes 2–4
actions: Abduction of toes 2–4 (away from the axis through the 2nd toe)
tip: ‘DAB’ — Dorsal ABduct; in the foot the reference line runs through the 2nd toe, not the 3rd as in the hand.

name: Plantar interossei
etymology: From Latin plantaris ‘of the sole’ + inter ‘between’ + ossa ‘bones’. So it means ‘the muscles between the bones, on the sole side’ — three unipennate muscles.
origin: Bases and medial sides of metatarsals 3–5
insertion: Medial sides of the bases of the proximal phalanges of toes 3–5
tip: ‘PAD’ — Plantar ADduct; three plantar vs four dorsal interossei.
